record.title: Mitochondrial oxidant production is source- and state-dependent
record.proposition: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
record.process: Codex bounded PM4/PM5 SEC completion v1: exact propositions, primary full-text recovery, factor-specific appraisal, scoped independence and explicit unresolved judgements; no human scientific-review status inferred.

methodology.name: Existing SEC four-factor anchors and integrated caps

rationale.D: Brand site-selective suppressors and Chouchani reperfusion perturbations test source generation, respiration and reverse-electron-transport endpoints in the stated experimental models (Brand Figs 1–2, 5; Chouchani Figs 2–4). No food or human efficacy proposition is scored.
rationale.B: Source counterscreens and respiration controls limit nonspecific inhibition, and reperfusion experiments add tracer/pharmacological checks. Tool selectivity and between-model transfer remain material residual concerns; this is not a fully bias-protected dietary trial.
rationale.P: Dose-response/selectivity and respiratory measurements discriminate source suppression from generalized inhibition. The limits of selectivity and translation across preparations leave uncertainty in effect size and applicable source boundaries; P2 is not established.
rationale.R: The two research programmes provide partially matching evidence for source-dependent complex-I oxidant regulation. They do not independently replicate every component of this composite Finding; multiple models within Brand are not counted as independent research-group replication.

record.capRationale: No D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies; adjusted equals raw. No extra model-to-human penalty is added because the proposition remains model-specific.
limitations: Experimental suppressors and ischaemia models establish source regulation, not dietary effectiveness. These results do not imply that all mitochondrial ROS are harmful or that mitochondrial emission assays isolate gross production.

targetedChecks.assessment: S1QEL compounds suppressed site-IQ superoxide/H2O2 without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation; protection was context-specific. Tool compounds are not dietary inputs; effects across models are not independent human replications.

Accumulated succinate oxidation on reperfusion drove complex-I reverse-electron-transport ROS and injury. Pathological reperfusion is not a meal experiment; the origin of ischaemic succinate has been debated in subsequent primary work. No dietary succinate advice follows.

record.title: High-fat exposure altered mitochondrial H2O2-emitting potential
record.proposition: A specified high-fat meal and short high-fat feeding period increased skeletal-muscle mitochondrial H2O2-emitting potential in a small human experiment; separate rodent perturbations supported a role for mitochondrial oxidants in insulin resistance.
record.process: Codex bounded PM4/PM5 SEC completion v1: exact propositions, primary full-text recovery, factor-specific appraisal, scoped independence and explicit unresolved judgements; no human scientific-review status inferred.

methodology.name: Existing SEC four-factor anchors and integrated caps

rationale.D: Anderson Fig. 6 tests the specified meal/short-feeding exposure and human muscle H2O2 emission. Its separate rodent interventions support the separately stated rodent clause, not human mediation.
rationale.B: Within-person baseline and validated emission/respirometry assays help attribution, but the sequential human feeding design lacks a randomized contemporaneous meal comparator; diet/time/order confounding remains. The scored statement is the observed experiment, not a causal replacement-diet claim.
rationale.P: Fig. 6 reports participant-level/sample-size context, mean/SEM and group comparisons; the rise is informative for the tested exposure. Nine men, assay-specific conditions and uncertain magnitude beyond this sample preclude P2. Rodent effects are not pooled with human precision.
rationale.R: Only one independent human feeding dataset supports the exact meal/five-day muscle-emission result in the bounded assessed body. The obese cross-section and rodent arms do not replicate that exposure/population proposition. R0 describes this scoped body, not proof of absence throughout the literature.

record.capRationale: No D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies; adjusted equals raw. No extra model-to-human penalty is added because the proposition remains model-specific.
limitations: Net H2O2 emission reflects production and scavenging under assay conditions. Human meal findings do not establish a specific ROS-generating site, benefit from a proposed replacement meal, effects of all dietary fats, brain outcomes or human causal mediation.

targetedChecks.assessment: After a meal providing >60% energy from fat and five days of high-fat feeding, muscle mitochondrial H2O2-emitting potential increased; rodent antioxidant manipulations preserved insulin sensitivity. The meal provided 35% of daily energy; post-meal biopsy was at four hours. Small non-randomised feeding sequence and assay-specific emission; rodent causality must not be assigned to the human cohort.

record.title: Inactivity and training changed mitochondrial H2O2 emission
record.proposition: Two weeks of leg immobilisation increased muscle mitochondrial H2O2 emission at a controlled membrane potential; six weeks of aerobic retraining restored emission and ATP-generating respiration toward baseline. Acute exercise responses were respiratory-state dependent in a separate study.
record.process: Codex bounded PM4/PM5 SEC completion v1: exact propositions, primary full-text recovery, factor-specific appraisal, scoped independence and explicit unresolved judgements; no human scientific-review status inferred.

methodology.name: Existing SEC four-factor anchors and integrated caps

rationale.D: Gram measures H2O2 emission at controlled membrane potential before immobilisation and after retraining; Fig. 9 directly matches the principal claim. The separate acute study supplies only the distinct respiratory-state-dependent clause.
rationale.B: Within-person measures and the contralateral-leg comparator address baseline differences. Sequential recovery/retraining and resumption of ordinary activity cannot be separated, and not all state-specific assays normalize similarly.
rationale.P: Gram Figs 8–10 show SEM and protocol-specific comparisons at fixed potential, supporting the scoped direction. Recovery varies by respiratory state, comparator-leg changes occur, and age/size estimates remain uncertain; P1 applies without claiming complete recovery in every state.
rationale.R: One independent immobilisation/retraining cohort carries the exact longitudinal claim. Young/older strata are not two research-group replications; the acute-exercise cohort tests a different protocol. R0 is for this explicitly bounded evidence body.

record.capRationale: No D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies; adjusted equals raw. No extra model-to-human penalty is added because the proposition remains model-specific.
limitations: Measured emission is not pure source production. Immobilisation/retraining does not establish a universal exercise dose or a brain/ADHD effect. Acute and chronic exercise effects must not be collapsed into “exercise lowers ROS”.

targetedChecks.assessment: Immobilisation increased H2O2 emission and reduced ATP-generating respiration; subsequent training reversed these changes. Sequential design; skeletal muscle only; antioxidant-enzyme changes may influence emission.

Acute exercise altered H2O2 emission in a respiratory-state-specific manner, including increases under one complex-I leak condition. Not a uniform decrease; exercise/insulin timing and substrates matter; no neurological outcome.

record.title: Vitamin E protection depends on tissue and stress context
record.proposition: Vitamin E deficiency and repletion experiments support a protective role for vitamin E in selected mitochondrial membranes. Mitochondrial-GPX4 loss in mice caused retinal lipid oxidation and photoreceptor loss partly ameliorated by vitamin E. Other rat liver experiments did not show the same dependence.
record.process: Codex bounded PM4/PM5 SEC completion v1: exact propositions, primary full-text recovery, factor-specific appraisal, scoped independence and explicit unresolved judgements; no human scientific-review status inferred.

methodology.name: Existing SEC four-factor anchors and integrated caps

rationale.D: The exact synthesis combines membrane protection, deficiency and retinal mitochondrial-GPX4 genetics. Rafique respiratory-chain activity and whole-retina lipid/photoreceptor rescue require an explicit bridge to local mitochondrial membrane protection; D1 preserves this inferential step.
rationale.B: Isoform-specific knockout/control comparisons, lipid assays and dietary rescue improve attribution. Small tissue/model samples, developmental effects and incomplete protection against allocation/litter-related confounding remain; tissue divergence is retained.
rationale.P: Azuma Figures 1–3 report replicate counts, variability and partial rescue with retained null cone endpoints; the direction is informative but rescue size and organelle-specific attribution remain uncertain. No numerical pooling across tissues.
rationale.R: Independent rat and mouse research lines give partial confirmation of context-dependent protective capacity with different endpoints. Liver nulls constrain rather than negate the tissue-qualified proposition; they do not warrant R2 universal protection.

record.capRationale: D1 ceiling 5 applies; raw 4 remains adjusted 4. No B0/P0 cap applies.
limitations: Capacity is not benefit from extra intake. Deficiency models, mitochondrial-GPX4 deletion and high supplemental exposure do not establish ordinary-food equivalence, uniform protection across tissues or cognitive benefit. Retinal lipid assays were not measurements restricted to isolated mitochondrial membranes.

targetedChecks.access: Primary abstract/article landing page recovered; scanned PDF methods/figures not extracted
targetedChecks.assessment: Muscle respiratory-chain activity decreased with deficiency, whereas liver activity increased; vitamin E deficiency did not exacerbate induced liver-particle peroxidation/inhibition under the tested conditions. Tissue divergence and the liver null are central; no universal mitochondrial requirement or human optimisation dose.

Photoreceptor loss and oxidised DHA-containing phosphatidylethanolamine increased; vitamin E partly rescued retinal degeneration. The enriched diet was 1000 IU/kg feed, not a human prescription. Tissue lipid oxidation and isoform-specific genetics do not establish a food intervention.

record.title: Mitochondrial glutathione requires compartmental transport
record.proposition: SLC25A39 perturbation and organelle uptake experiments establish that mitochondrial glutathione depends on import. Precursor supply, cytosolic synthesis, mitochondrial transport and local glutathione use are separate steps.
record.process: Codex bounded PM4/PM5 SEC completion v1: exact propositions, primary full-text recovery, factor-specific appraisal, scoped independence and explicit unresolved judgements; no human scientific-review status inferred.

methodology.name: Existing SEC four-factor anchors and integrated caps

rationale.D: Wang and Shi directly measure mitochondrial GSH and isotope-labelled organelle uptake after SLC25A39 perturbation. The scored proposition is compartmental import, not GSH antioxidant efficacy, dietary precursor success or clinical protection.
rationale.B: Independent genetic perturbations, cDNA rescue, tag/background controls, organelle separation, isotope uptake time courses and structure-function mutants address off-target, contamination and indirect synthesis explanations (Wang Fig. 3; Shi Figs 4–5). These are design-appropriate protections for this biochemical proposition.
rationale.P: Uptake contrasts, time courses and rescue/mutant comparisons with independent biological samples and LC-MS quality controls resolve the qualitative presence of an import dependency. The decision boundary is discrimination from intact uptake after knockout or merely cytosolic depletion; no precise human flux is inferred.
rationale.R: Wang (Birsoy group) and Shi (Shen group) independently establish the same SLC25A39/GSH-import relationship with distinct screens and uptake experiments. Colell is context for transport limitations, not a third SLC25A39 replication.

record.capRationale: No D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies; adjusted equals raw. No extra model-to-human penalty is added because the proposition remains model-specific.
limitations: Glutathione-dependent iron–sulfur-cluster maintenance is not interchangeable with peroxide detoxification. Cytosolic or blood glutathione does not establish mitochondrial delivery; in ethanol-fed rats NAC failed to restore mitochondrial GSH whereas SAM supplementation did.

targetedChecks.assessment: SLC25A39 was required to maintain mitochondrial GSH; experiments highlighted iron–sulfur-cluster biology rather than establishing antioxidant buffering as the sole essential function. Not an oral precursor trial; organelle GSH concentration is not protective flux.

SLC25A39 loss impaired GSH import and OXPHOS; intramitochondrial labelled GSSG supported use of imported GSH. GSSG labelling does not isolate GPX4 activity or prove protection from a dietary precursor.

targetedChecks.assessment: SAM restored mitochondrial GSH after ethanol feeding; NAC did not. Specific ethanol-induced membrane/transport impairment; not evidence that NAC never works or that ordinary sulfur foods are ineffective.

record.title: SOD2 metal occupancy affects mitochondrial protein injury
